tip: Hindi puts is/are at the very end: है (hai) or हैं (hain). मेरी बहन डॉक्टर है (meri behen doctor hai) – literally 'my sister doctor is'.
Question words sit in the answer's slot: in कैसे हो (kaise ho = how are you), कैसे (kaise) fills the spot the answer ठीक (theek = fine) would take – no flipping to the front like English.
Possessives match the thing owned, not the owner: तुम्हारे बच्चे (tumhare bachche = your children) – तुम्हारे (tumhare) is plural because बच्चे is, whoever you are.
The verb ending shows the speaker's own gender: a man says पीता हूँ (peeta hun = I drink), a woman says पीती हूँ (peeti hun). Same I, different ending.
There's no verb 'to know' here – knowledge sits on you: मुझे नहीं पता (mujhe nahin pata) is literally 'to me it is not known'. मुझे (mujhe = to me) does the work.
Third-person verbs mark gender too: वह जाती है (vah jaati hai = she goes) has -ती because she's female; a boy would be जाता है (jaata hai).
No matter how long the sentence, the verb comes last: time, place and object all pile up before साथ देते हैं (saath dete hain = stand by), which waits at the end.
With पसंद है (pasand hai = is pleasing), the liker takes को (ko): बेटी को पसंद है (beti ko pasand hai) is literally 'to the daughter it is pleasing', not 'daughter likes'.
Masculine -ा words shift to -े before a position word: बजा (baja) becomes बजे (baje) before तक (tak = by) – ढाई बजे तक (dhai baje tak = by two-thirty).
से (se) means 'from' but also handles 'than': सौ से अधिक (sau se adhik = more than a hundred) is literally 'from a hundred, more'.
को (ko) marks a definite object: बक्से को (bakse ko) means that specific heavy box. Drop को and it reads like some box or other.
Position words follow their noun: कल तक (kal tak) is literally 'tomorrow by' = 'by tomorrow'. Flip the English order every time.
ही (hi) narrows to 'only/exactly': मुझसे ही होगा (mujhse hi hoga) = it will get done only by me. It's sharper than English 'just'.
तो (to) adds attitude – contrast or emphasis, like 'well' or 'really': तुमने तो कमाल कर दिया (tumne to kamaal kar diya) = you really pulled it off.
भी (bhi = also/too) sits right after the word it stresses: तुम भी चलो (tum bhi chalo) = you come too. Move भी and the emphasis moves with it.
के (ke) + a word builds two-part position words: के लिए (ke liye = for), as in मेहमानों के लिए (mehmaanon ke liye = for the guests). Learn each pair as one chunk.
Verb + के लिए (ke liye) means 'in order to': जाना (jaana = to go) shifts to जाने in जाने के लिए (jaane ke liye = in order to go).
के साथ (ke saath) = physically 'with': परिवार के साथ (parivaar ke saath = with his family). Don't mix it up with के पास (ke paas), which means 'near' or 'have'.
Adding जी (ji) shows respect or warmth: दादाजी (dadaji = respected grandfather). Elders often get it built in – पिताजी (pitaji), माताजी (mataji).
